articles.title: 5 tips for getting the most out of AI
articles.description: Why do some people seem to be getting a lot out of AI, while others—maybe you—still feel like they’re spinning their wheels trying to squeeze anything remotely useful out of these platforms? The answer is multifaceted, of course. Some workflows are better suited to the strengths of large language models, while others are more vulnerable to their weaknesses. Some users pay for upgraded plans, which can improve how well the models work. But a big part of the difference comes down to how you use artificial intelligence. Like any tool, there are ways to make it perform better for you. In other words, the technology is often what you make of it. If you offload your thinking to AI platforms, you risk dulling your ability to approach problems creatively and becoming dependent on a flawed technological crutch. But if you use AI to challenge yourself, stress-test your work, and outsource routine tasks, you might feel, at least in some sense, like you’ve gotten a significant upgrade. Consider the calculator: Some people have become so reliant on it that their mental math skills suffer, while others use the technology to tackle more advanced math because they’re not spending their time on simpler problems. Like all new technologies, what you choose to outsource to AI is up to you. Still, if you do decide to use it, it’s worth considering how to get the most out of the technology—and make sure chatbots serve you, rather than the other way around. Here are a few tips to make these platforms work better for you. Be smart about your prompts What you type into your AI actually matters. Take traditional search engines. You may not realize it, but over time, you might have developed an implicit sense of how using certain Boolean operators or more specific proper nouns can yield better, more relevant results to your queries. The same is true for AI. Being more specific with a chatbot about what information you want can make a big difference, particularly when you’re using the technology as a search tool. It might be easy to slip into thinking that AI should already know what you want, but it doesn’t. Instead, treat a chatbot as an earnest research assistant with the capacity to make a lot of mistakes. There’s an old adage: “The more you know, the more they know.” The same logic applies to AI. Here’s an example: If I’m shopping for a bookshelf, I no longer sift through countless listings searching for something that feels right. Instead, I take a picture of the spot where I need it to go, give the AI the dimensions (or range of dimensions) I’m looking for, and ask the chatbot to find the best options given those constraints. This saves me a lot of time and allows me to work smarter when using AI for shopping. Encourage humility One of the big problems with AI—or any work you don’t do yourself and instead outsource to someone (or something) else—is that it will make mistakes. Fear of an AI oopsie is anxiety-inducing and absolutely real, and one of the best reasons not to completely offload all your tasks to ChatGPT or Claude. Really, don’t do this! The best approach is to check any work produced by a chatbot yourself. But there are also ways to help these tools work better. If you have the ability to adjust your AI’s settings, tell it to be more humble—and more cautious—when sharing information or making claims. Tell your AI to consider multiple ways of thinking about a question or problem, and to present divergent viewpoints. For kicks, tell it to admit when it’s unsure. Also, always ask for direct citations and check them off the platform. When you send a prompt to your chatbot, tell it to avoid simply summarizing information and instead to provide direct links to sources so you can verify the claims yourself. Once you do this, you might be shocked by how often AI claims to be consulting a source or generates a fake web page only to apologize when you discover it doesn’t actually exist. A polite reminder: Just because Claude says it’s “double-checking” something doesn’t mean it actually is. You need to double-check it, too! AI can cite unreliable sources and even hallucinate citations entirely. AI is powerful, but also unpredictable, and should never be treated as an objective source of information. Think of it as a sieve that helps you sift through information and find what you want faster, rather than something you can trust to identify the best results on its own. Understand memory Your AI is remembering what you ask it and what you tell it, even if you’re not always aware. This isn’t necessarily unique to AI systems; many tech platforms collect all sorts of data about you and then use that information to tailor content to you (usually, ads). It’s possible you don’t want AI to remember anything about you at all, in which case, check your privacy settings—or perhaps avoid AI entirely. But if you are comfortable with a chatbot retaining information about you, consider that its memory can actually be a useful tool. For instance, if you’re using AI to draft emails, tell your chatbot to always introduce you in the way you prefer. If you tend to offer to jump on a call or Zoom, tell the AI that you like doing so—and ask it to remember that preference for when you draft emails in the future. If you prefer a more casual tone, tell it that. If you prefer to remain formal, tell it that instead. Here’s another example: If you’d like your AI to avoid sending you links from Amazon when you’re online shopping—perhaps you don’t have an Amazon account—tell it to remember that preference so you don’t have to keep sifting through those links. Or maybe you’d prefer your AI to prioritize links to The New York Times because you already have a subscription. Tell your AI that, too. Also, remember that you don’t need to give AI your personal information at all. For kicks, try asking it to erase things from its memory that you don’t want it to retain. There’s absolutely no guarantee that a request alone will erase the information completely, so check your privacy and memory settings, too. But why not give it a stab? Customize how AI communicates You spend a lot of time on Google, but you might now be pivoting to AI to surface information instead. One advantage of this is that you can have AI produce results in all sorts of formats and styles, since you dictate the terms in which it expresses itself. For instance, you might prefer to receive information in simple bullet points rather than a long, essay-like string of text. You can share that preference with your chatbot. Maybe you prefer visuals and graphics? AI is great at whipping those up. For the nerds: Maybe you prefer receiving information in code that you can then copy and paste into a development environment, like Python, so you can run a script to check whatever work the AI did in a more deterministic way. There are even simpler changes you could make. You might prefer that AI respond in two languages, perhaps because you already know one but are working on developing your skills in the other. Seeing the text side by side as you interact with the platform throughout the day might help boost your fluency. Another example: I’ve instructed my AI to regularly incorporate more unusual, niche vocabulary. There’s a somewhat well-founded fear that AI is homogenizing our language and making us less creative in how we express ourselves. I told AI to reverse that trend and gave it a list of common AI crutch words to avoid. Know your way around tokens AI operates on tokens. You spend input tokens on the information you give a model, including your prompts and relevant context, and output tokens on what it produces in response. You may not always know how many tokens you’ve used, but writing long prompts generally means using more input tokens, while receiving long responses means using more output tokens. As you employ chatbots and run up against usage limits, consider that you can guide your AI on how much detail to provide for a particular task. Tell it to be brief when you want a short response or just one link, and tell it when you want a really detailed answer.

articles.title: Why two identical Galaxy phones can run different firmware versions
articles.description: Why two identical Galaxy phones can run different firmware versions Two Galaxy phones can look identical, share the same model name on the box, and sit on the same table, yet one runs a newer firmware version than the other. It feels like a mistake. It usually is not. Samsung ships the same phone in many slightly different forms, and each form follows its own update path. The model name on the box is not the whole story A Galaxy S24 is not one phone. It is a family of phones that share a name. Different regions get different processors, different modems, and different hardware revisions, and Samsung gives each variant its own model number. A phone sold in the US might be SM-S921U, while the same name in Europe is SM-S921B. The letters at the end matter more than the name on the front. Firmware is built for a specific model number, not for a marketing name. An update released for the SM-S921B does nothing for the SM-S921U, because the two phones run different builds with different drivers. When two owners compare versions and find a mismatch, the first thing to check is the full model number in Settings, under About phone. If the last letters differ, the phones were never on the same update track to begin with. Even within one model number, there are hardware revisions. A phone built in one factory batch can carry a different modem revision than another, and Samsung sometimes splits updates by revision. The differences are invisible from the outside, but the update server sees them. Your region code sets your update schedule Every Samsung phone carries a CSC code, which is the region code for the country or carrier it was sold in. The CSC decides which firmware build the phone receives, because Samsung releases updates country by country rather than all at once. A phone with a German CSC and a phone with an Indian CSC are on different release schedules even when the hardware is the same. Carrier phones add another layer. A phone bought from a carrier gets firmware that the carrier has tested and approved, and carriers test at different speeds. An unlocked phone often gets an update weeks before the same model on a carrier network, simply because there is no carrier approval step in the way. The phone is not broken or forgotten. It is waiting in a different queue. This is also why a phone bought in one country and used in another can seem stuck. Its CSC still points at the country it was sold in, so it follows that country's schedule, not the schedule of the country it now lives in. Security patches and feature updates move at different speeds Not every version difference means the same thing. Samsung releases monthly security patches and larger feature updates on separate tracks. A phone can be behind on one and current on the other, and two phones can differ on both for different reasons. Security patches roll out in waves over several weeks. Samsung does not push a patch to every phone on the same day, partly to control server load and partly so a bad patch can be stopped before it reaches everyone. A two week gap between two phones on the same model and region is normal during a rollout. Feature updates are slower still. A major Android version upgrade is released in stages, and Samsung often holds it back for specific regions or carriers while early problems are fixed. The phone that got it first is not luckier in any lasting sense. The other phone usually catches up within a few weeks, unless its variant has a genuine delay. The update server checks more than your model When a phone checks for updates, Samsung's servers look at the model number, the CSC, the carrier, the current build, and the bootloader version. Each of those can hold an update back. A phone on an older bootloader version cannot jump straight to a build that needs a newer one, so it waits for an intermediate update first. A phone that skipped several updates may need to take them in order rather than leaping to the latest. Rooted phones and phones with modified software are another case. Samsung's update system can refuse to serve an update to a phone whose software has been changed, because the update is built on the assumption of stock firmware. The phone reports that it is up to date, even when newer firmware exists for its model, because as far as the server is concerned, that phone is no longer on the standard track. Battery level and storage can also delay a visible update. A phone will not offer a large update when its storage is nearly full or its battery is low, and the update simply does not appear until those conditions change. What to do when your phone seems behind Start with the facts. Check the full model number and the CSC code, and compare them with the other phone, not just the marketing name. If the model numbers differ, there is nothing to fix. The phones run different firmware by design. If the model and CSC match and the gap is more than a few weeks, check whether the phone is carrier locked, whether its software has been modified, and whether it has enough free storage. A manual check in Settings, then Software update, then Download and install is worth trying, since the automatic check runs on its own schedule. Flashing firmware manually can bring a phone up to date, but it only works when the firmware matches the exact model number and CSC. Flashing a build meant for a different variant is how phones get bricked, so the model number check comes first, every time. A version gap between two phones that look the same is usually a sign that they are not the same phone underneath, or that they are standing in different queues. Once you know which queue your phone is in, the gap stops being a mystery. For official firmware downloads, visit SamFware, where SamFware also publishes step-by-step Odin guides for every Galaxy model.

articles.title: Building StareBrain, Part 17: Drag-to-Reposition and Persisting Overlay Position
articles.description: Building StareBrain, Part 17: Drag-to-Reposition and Persisting Overlay Position Part 16 introduced the overlay window — the floating UI layer that shows task progress and surfaces confirmation prompts. One problem we hit immediately in testing: the overlay covers UI the user needs to interact with. The fix is drag-to-reposition. The user holds and drags the overlay anywhere on screen. When they reopen StareBrain, it's where they left it. Here's how we built it. Touch Handling The overlay uses a View. OnTouchListener to track drag gestures. We calculate delta from the initial touch position and update WindowManager. LayoutParams on every ACTION_MOVE. class OverlayView(context: Context) : FrameLayout(context) { private private private private var onPositionChanged: ((Int, Int) -> Unit)? = null init { setOnTouchListener { _, event -> val params = layoutParams as WindowManager. LayoutParams when (event.action) { MotionEvent.ACTION_DOWN -> { initialX = params.x initialY = params.y initialTouchX = event.rawX initialTouchY = event.rawY true } MotionEvent.ACTION_MOVE -> { val dx = (event.rawX - initialTouchX).toInt() val dy = (event.rawY - initialTouchY).toInt() params.x = initialX + dx params.y = initialY + dy val wm = context.getSystemService(WindowManager::class.java) MotionEvent.ACTION_UP -> { val params2 = layoutParams as WindowManager. LayoutParams onPositionChanged?.invoke(params2.x, params2.y) else -> false onPositionChanged fires on ACTION_UP — once the drag is complete, not on every pixel. This avoids thrashing the persistence layer during the move. Distinguishing Drag from Tap A short touch that doesn't move should still register as a tap (expand/collapse, confirm/reject). We distinguish by checking displacement: val dx = event.rawX - initialTouchX val dy = event.rawY - initialTouchY val displacement = Math.sqrt((dx * dx + dy * dy).toDouble()) else { companion object { private const val DRAG_THRESHOLD_PX = 10f Under 10px of movement → tap. Over 10px → drag and persist. Persisting Position via SessionMemory We store overlay position in SessionMemory alongside behavioral patterns. Position is not sensitive data — it's a UI preference. data class OverlayPosition( val x: Int, val y: Int ) class SessionMemory(private val context: Context) { private val prefs = context.getSharedPreferences("session_memory", Context.MODE_PRIVATE) fun saveOverlayPosition(position: OverlayPosition) { .putInt("overlay_x", position.x) .putInt("overlay_y", position.y) .apply() fun loadOverlayPosition(): OverlayPosition { val x = prefs.getInt("overlay_x", DEFAULT_X) val y = prefs.getInt("overlay_y", DEFAULT_Y) return OverlayPosition(x, y) private const val DEFAULT_X = 16 private const val DEFAULT_Y = 120 Restoring Position on Launch In OverlayManager.show(), we load the saved position before adding the view: fun show() { val savedPosition = sessionMemory.loadOverlayPosition() val params = WindowManager. LayoutParams( WindowManager. LayoutParams.WRAP_CONTENT, WindowManager. LayoutParams.TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY, WindowManager. LayoutParams.FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE or WindowManager. LayoutParams.FLAG_LAYOUT_NO_LIMITS, PixelFormat.TRANSLUCENT ).apply { gravity = Gravity.TOP or Gravity.START x = savedPosition.x y = savedPosition.y overlayView = OverlayView(context).also { view -> view.onPositionChanged = { x, y -> Note the gravity change: Gravity.TOP or Gravity.START instead of TOP or END. When we save absolute x/y coordinates, we need a fixed anchor — START gives us that. END would mirror the offset and place the overlay in the wrong position after a restore. Screen Boundary Clamping If the user's screen resolution changes (rotation, different device), the saved position might be off-screen. We clamp on restore: fun loadOverlayPosition(displayMetrics: DisplayMetrics): OverlayPosition { val clampedX = x.coerceIn(0, displayMetrics.widthPixels - OVERLAY_WIDTH_PX) val clampedY = y.coerceIn(0, displayMetrics.heightPixels - OVERLAY_HEIGHT_PX) return OverlayPosition(clampedX, clampedY) What's Next Part 18 will cover auto-collapse: the overlay shrinks to a dot when the user is actively interacting with another app, and expands when a step completes or confirmation is needed — without interrupting what the user is doing.

articles.title: How I Put Three AI Agents in a Discord Channel with Switch (and What Broke on Windows)
articles.description: I built ShipLoop for the Flip the Switch hackathon. It takes a customer complaint in Discord to a tested GitHub pull request, and a human makes the merge decision. This post covers what I built, how to set it up, and the problems I hit as a first-time Switch user on Windows. Demo video: https://youtu.be/ueEJwIVH1A4 Repo: https://github.com/Jatin083/shiploop The problem Customer bug reports often get stuck between support and engineering. Someone has to understand the report, reproduce it, fix it, review it and update the customer. Every handoff adds delay. What ShipLoop does Three Claude Code agents share one chat room: Triager classifies the report and hands bugs to Fixer, using the customer's exact words. Fixer reproduces the bug, writes a failing test, makes the fix and opens a pull request. Reviewer checks the pull request with its own edge-case tests. I merge on GitHub and tell Triager. Triager then reports the elapsed time and drafts a customer update for my approval. The demo app is a small FastAPI shop with deliberately planted bugs. Nothing is deployed to a live site, and the customer updates were drafts that were not sent. What is Switch? Switch puts AI agents into team chat. A channel becomes a room, and agents join it like teammates. Switch does not ship its own agent or model. You bring an agent such as Claude Code, and Switch connects it to the room. Setup 1. Install the tools. You need Switch Console, Docker Desktop and an AI coding agent. Sign in to Claude Code: claude auth login 2. Start Docker first. Then, in Switch Console, select Add a server and Run a server on this computer. I started once with Docker off. The server ran, but without its bundled Mattermost chat app. 3. Test one agent. Use the Switch expert template and turn on Start it in a room. Mention the agent by its exact name. An agent ignores a message that does not address it. 4. Create your agents. Go to Your Agents, then add each one with a name, a working directory and instructions. I gave Reviewer its own clone of the repo, so it would not switch branches under Fixer. 5. Connect Discord. Create a bot in the Discord Developer Portal and turn on Server Members Intent and Message Content Intent. Invite the bot with the permissions in the Switch guide. Then connect it from Home > Messaging apps. Keep the bot token secret. 6. Add rules to the room. My instructions say that only the human merges, and that nothing goes to a customer without approval. 7. Check before you start. These two room commands show the state of the room: !agents-status !roles What broke, and what fixed it Claude Code showed "CLI not installed". The same panel had found its version, and agents still ran. It looked like a Windows path check problem, so reinstalling would not have helped. "Address already in use", but nothing was using the port. Windows had reserved that port range. You can check with: netsh interface ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp Quit Docker Desktop and Switch Console, then run these as administrator: net stop winnat net start winnat Handoff between two rooms failed. I first planned separate support and engineering rooms. The agent's connection call reported success, but its message to the other agent was refused with Targets not in room. Moving all the agents into one room solved it. Agents replied in the logs, but not in Discord. The bot needed the Manage Webhooks permission. Roles were held somewhere else. An agent can hold one role lease at a time, so old rooms can block a new one. Check with !roles. Mentions wake agents. Even an @mention inside quoted text wakes an agent and uses tokens. I now leave off the @ in setup messages. The result Two runs on Discord ended in merged pull requests: Bug Pull request Tests after the fix Report to human merge Duplicate cancellation #6 41 passed 3m 6s Cart quantity #8 42 passed 5m 53s In both runs, the new regression test failed on the old code before the fix. What I learned Prove one agent first. Getting Fixer to open one real pull request removed the biggest risk. Keep the workflow in one room until you have tested handoffs across rooms. Say where the human decides. My agents are told never to merge, but GitHub branch protection is not turned on. A real team should enforce it. Be honest about limits. Concurrent requests can still produce wrong counts in the demo app. If you try Switch, start with one agent and one channel, then add the next agent after that works. I used Claude Code to help build this project and write this post. HowISwitch

articles.title: What ‘Woke 3’ could mean for the workplace
articles.description: In the aftermath of the Democrats sweeping the midterms, the internet has anointed this moment “Woke 3.0”: an extension of the terminology that people have used to describe the political and cultural movement that took hold during the pandemic, particularly after George Floyd’s murder. It’s something that was recently referenced by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in a widely discussed interview where she appeared to distance herself from that brand of progressivism. (As she put it: “Woke 1 was crazy.”) On social media this week, the discourse around Woke 3.0 has taken the form of quips about pronouns and anti-AI rhetoric. But this discussion, unserious though it may be, captures how the outcome of the election could have real implications for diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts in the workplace. Back in 2020, it seemed like corporate America was finally taking DEI seriously. Some of the biggest tech employers in the country—among them Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta—didn’t just speak out about the racial reckoning but also backed up those commitments with hundreds of millions of dollars. Many companies hired chief diversity officers for the first time and, at least on the surface, appeared to make real investments in DEI talent. It didn’t take long for that to change—first quietly, then more publicly as the Trump administration set its sights on the DEI movement and the Supreme Court struck down affirmative action. As the public outcry over racial injustice faded, companies started to divest from DEI programs. In retrospect, it seems obvious that some companies merely paid lip service to diversity efforts; as Fast Company has reported, many employers were so hasty in their attempts to publicly support DEI that they didn’t ensure there was enough structural support for those initiatives, or any real way of measuring progress. When the climate shifted, it was relatively easy for some of them to deprioritize those efforts. Many DEI leaders also found themselves burnt out and tired of constantly agitating for change in the face of so much resistance. So what could the next era—Woke 3.0, to borrow a phrase—mean for DEI in the workplace? Some of the Trump administration’s anti-DEI actions simply cannot be reversed overnight, or at all until the White House changes hands. Trump’s executive orders have slashed DEI programs across the federal government and eliminated affirmative action requirements for any number of employers who are federal contractors. Since the start of his second term, Trump has taken steps to compromise the authority and independence of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whose mission is to enforce anti-discrimination laws. With Andrea Lucas at the helm, the agency has focused intensely on snuffing out DEI programs, targeting private sector companies like Nike over their diversity efforts and pushing to scrap EEO-1 data collection, which has required most employers to provide demographic data on their workforce for six decades. It could take years to unwind the damage. That aside, it’s not clear how much of an appetite employers currently have for DEI work. As diversity experts and advocates have previously told Fast Company, there are plenty of companies that never stopped doing this work, even if they didn’t talk about it openly; some of them renamed those efforts, opting for terms like belonging. But there are other companies for whom this is likely no longer a priority—if it ever was. With so many companies now fixated on AI and what that will mean for their workforce, it’s hard to imagine there will be a broad, renewed commitment to DEI across corporate America. When companies conduct layoffs, as so many employers have been, HR and DEI roles are often the first to go. The AI boom may simply present yet another hurdle for the DEI practitioners who have had to fight to be taken seriously all along.
